articles.title: In Mississippi, researchers added waste wool to plant pots; basil yields reached up to 5 times the control, while Swiss chard yields reached up to 5 times the control
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking study in Mississippi, researchers found that adding waste sheep's wool to potting mixtures significantly increased basil and Swiss chard yields, achieving up to five times more than control plants. This article explores the implications of using wool as a nutrient source in agriculture.
articles.body: Basil and Swiss chard produced larger harvests because of the addition of waste sheep’s wool in a greenhouse experiment that was conducted by researchers in Mississippi. The plants were grown in potting mixtures that contained uncomposted wool waste, and total basil yields reached five times the control, and Swiss chard yields reached the same level across multiple harvests. Researchers Valtcho D. Zheljazkov and colleagues tested four amounts of wool in eight-inch pots, compared the results with plants grown without it, and assessed whether discarded wool could serve as a source of nutrients and a component of growing media.The plants were harvested several timesThe researchers added 20, 40, 80, or 120 grams of wool waste to each pot, and tested wool with perlite, wool with peat, and wool with a combination of peat and perlite. They also harvested basil five times during the experiment, while Swiss chard was harvested four times, and across those harvests, basil produced between 1.6 and five times the total yield of the untreated control, while Swiss chard produced between two and five times the control yield. The results covered the combined harvests, and also varied with the amount of wool and the growing mixture that was used. The study therefore does not establish that every wool treatment produced a fivefold increase or that the same result would occur in open fields.Wool supplied nutrients as it broke downThe researchers found higher nitrogen levels in the tissues of basil and Swiss chard that were grown with wool, and the growing media also contained higher levels of nitrate nitrogen and ammonium nitrogen, which are two forms that can be absorbed by plants. Wool is made largely of keratin, which is a protein that contains nitrogen and sulfur, and its fibres break down over time. Microscopic examination at the end of the experiment found that some fibres had decomposed while others retained the majority of their original surface structure.Researchers also observed plant roots that grew directly on wool fibres, and suggested that roots might grow towards nutrient-rich areas or that root activity could help break down the material. A later review of research on wool recycling in agriculture described waste wool as a potential source of nitrogen and sulfur, and also stated that its use depends on the crop, growing conditions, and method of application. The review was published in Agronomy in 2025, and also discusses how it can be used to amend soil and growing material.The results do not apply to every cropThe Mississippi experiment focused on two plants grown in containers, and its findings cannot establish how raw wool would affect vegetables, grains, or other crops grown in different soils and climates. Also, adding a material that releases nutrients gradually is not the same as applying a standard fertiliser at a measured rate, and growers would need to account for the crop’s nutrient requirements, the properties of the growing medium and how quickly the wool decomposes.A separate study published in the Journal of Environmental Management in 2020 examined sheep-farming by-products in barley production, wherein researchers reported that applying wool led to an increase in soil organic carbon and nitrogen, and produced higher barley yields than untreated plots. The field conditions and treatment methods were different from the Mississippi pot experiment, so the results are not directly comparable. The study provides additional evidence that wool waste may have agricultural uses beyond container-grown plants. The Mississippi findings show that uncomposted wool can support substantial yields in certain mixtures that grow in containers, and further work is needed to determine suitable application rates, how the material performs over longer periods and whether the gains hold across other crops and growing conditions.You use AI every day. articles.title: In Mississippi, researchers mixed raw sheep’s wool into soil; foxglove yields rose to 1.7–3.5 times the untreated plots over two growing seasons.
articles.summary: Research in Mississippi demonstrates that mixing raw sheep's wool into soil can significantly boost the yield of purple foxglove plants, enhancing harvests by up to 3.5 times over two growing seasons. This innovative method of utilizing wool waste as a slow-release nutrient source paves the way for sustainable agricultural practices.
articles.body: It was found that uncomposted sheep’s wool led to an increased yield of purple foxglove plants in a field experiment, with harvests reaching between 1.7 and 3.5 times the output of untreated plots. Two growing seasons were observed, and the researchers examined whether they could use wool waste to supply nutrients to high-value plants instead of discarding it.The research was published in Agronomy Journal in 2008 by Valtcho D. Zheljazkov and colleagues, who used wool waste at two application rates, 15.8 and 31.7 tonnes per hectare, alongside untreated soil for comparison. The researchers measured plant yields over the following two seasons.Wool released nutrients as it broke downSheep’s wool contains nitrogen and other elements that plants need, and unlike a soluble fertiliser, raw wool does not break down immediately after being mixed into the soil. The researchers found that some of the material was able to retain its original structure after two growing seasons and several harvests. Soil that was treated with wool had higher levels of ammonium and nitrate, which are two forms of nitrogen available to plants, and increases in nitrogen and protein concentrations in plant tissue were also recorded by the researchers, along with greater soil microbial biomass. The results suggest that wool can release nutrients over time as it undergoes decomposition, which may help supply plants across more than one harvest, although the amount that has been released depends on the material, application rate and growing conditions.The experiment focused on a high-value plantThe field trial used purple foxglove, or Digitalis purpurea, which is a plant grown for compounds used in medicines. The study mainly looked at foxglove, and whether raw wool would have the same effect on vegetables, grains or other crops remains unclear. The study also included pot experiments with other high-value plants, such as pot marigold and valerian, and those experiments found increased yields after wool or human hair waste was added to the soil. The field results, however, came from the foxglove trial.A separate study that was published in the Journal of Environmental Quality in 2005 also examined uncomposted wool and hair waste as soil amendments, and found that these materials could act as slow-release sources of nutrients and help in improving some soil chemical and biological properties. The authors also wanted to look into application rates and environmental effects, including the risk of nitrate leaching.More research is needed before general recommendationsThe researchers tested very specific amounts of wool in a particular crop, and the findings cannot automatically be applied to other soils or growing conditions. The original paper also found that high wool application rates changed the composition of soil microbial communities, while at the lower rate, the researchers did not observe the same change that is relative to untreated soil. The material's effects depended in part on how much was added.Research that was published in the Journal of Environmental Management in 2020 found that several measures of soil fertility were improved and barley grain and dry-fodder yields were increased by 50% compared with untreated plots. The experiment was conducted under its own soil and growing conditions, so it provides supporting evidence for further investigation instead of a direct comparison with the Mississippi foxglove trial.These studies, together, suggest that discarded wool could serve as a source of plant nutrients, but using it practically depends on the crop, soil, quantity applied, and environmental effects. The Mississippi experiment showed that foxglove yields increased over two growing seasons; it did not establish that raw wool can replace conventional fertilisers across agriculture.You use AI every day. articles.summary: KOLKATA: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday ordered an investigation into the role of temporary home guards deployed at a Kolkata puja
articles.body: KOLKATA: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday ordered an investigation into the role of temporary home guards deployed at a Kolkata puja pandal where a stampede on Saturday killed 19 people.Taking a swipe at the previous TMC government, Adhikari also said his administration was carrying the “baggage of rubbish” left behind by the erstwhile regime.Nineteen people died and 25 were injured in the stampede at Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata, following a crowd surge amid rain on Saturday evening.The CM said he had sought the list of temporary home guards deployed at the puja pandal to investigate their role in the stampede."These home guards are not new recruits. They were on duty for the third year in a row, following their earlier appointments in 2024 and 2025," he told news agency PTI."We are carrying on our shoulders a massive pile of rubbish as baggage. A clean-up will take time," Adhikari asserted.He pointed out that one of the home guards he tried to talk to at the pandal early this morning "could not even understand, let alone speak, Bengali"."My views about the disaster changed after I visited the site, compared to what I was initially briefed. The accident took place at the common entry and exit gate, and not inside the puja pandal, which was dimly lit. I shudder to think of the consequences if this had happened inside. No one knows where the death toll would have reached," Adhikari said.He said that, instead of separate entry and exit gates, a single opening divided by a rope held by home guards served both purposes."When it started to rain, they simply dropped the ropes and took shelter to save themselves from getting drenched," the chief minister claimed, suggesting that an absence of an entry-exit divide led to the commotion spiraling out of control.Adhikari, though, added that the role of the puja organisers and permission-issuing authorities will also be probed."The organisers will also have to shoulder responsibility. There were problems with the theme as well. We are keeping under the scanner the Kolkata Police and fire services department, which issued the necessary licenses and should have had these issues rectified beforehand," he said.Adhikari also said that personnel of the Kolkata Police, Kolkata Municipal Corporation and fire services department have been kept out of the Special Investigation Team (SIT), which will be headed by a sitting judge of the Calcutta High Court, provided the state receives the nod of the Chief Justice.Kolkata Pandal stampede: Seven accused remanded to 10-day police custodyThe Bankshal Court on Sunday remanded seven people arrested in connection with the Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal stampede to 10 days of police custody. Police had sought 14 days of custody.Defence lawyer MD Yashim Raheman claimed that the accused were outsiders who had come to witness the Puja celebrations.He said the court had granted custody until October 28, while police had sought remand until November 1."We informed the court that these individuals were outsiders; they had come to witness the Durga Puja celebrations. Upon observing the heavy crowding--where many people were in distress--they stepped in to assist with rescue efforts...Regarding the police custody (PC), the court has granted it until the 28th. Everyone has been remanded to police custody until the 28th. The police had requested custody until the 1st, but the judge granted it until the 28th," he told news agency ANI.Rain, overcrowding and narrow space contributed to stampede: LocalsResidents of Kolkata’s Chorbagan area on Sunday blamed sudden rainfall, limited space, heavy crowds and inadequate deployment of volunteers and police for the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal that claimed 19 lives on Saturday.They said the rain forced visitors inside the pandal to wait for the weather to improve, while those waiting outside grew restless and tried to enter the already overcrowded marquee.Pramod Gupta, who lives near the Chorbagan puja pandal on Radha Madhav Lane, said the queue of visitors stretched up to Mahatma Gandhi Road, around 700 metres away.“Everything was fine till the rain started,” he said.Gupta said the downpour triggered a sudden rush, with people inside trying to leave the pandal as more visitors pushed in from outside.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: ‘Where did the 56-inch chest go?’ Rahul targets PM Modi, Shah in Goa, says BJP’s ‘expiry date’ is near
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Sunday said Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Sunday said Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would face justice over alleged “vote chori”. Rahul also declared that the BJP’s “expiry date” was approaching.Addressing a public meeting in Margao, Goa, Rahul accused the BJP leadership of alleged electoral malpractice, corruption and targeting student protesters, while urging voters to give the Congress a full majority in the 2027 Assembly elections.“Gyanesh Kumar implements the theft of votes, Amit Shah operationalizes it, and Narendra Modi orchestrates the entire plan from behind the scenes,” Rahul said.He questioned why no defamation case had been filed against him specifically over his allegations of vote theft. “I am facing over 45 defamation cases—cases filed by Amit Shah, by Narendra Modi, and so on. Despite these 45 cases, I continue to state at every opportunity that Narendra Modi steals votes. Yet, no case has been filed against me specifically for this claim,” he said.Calling the Congress a protector of the Constitution, Gandhi said the three leaders would be held accountable.“Gyanesh Kumar knows that these people cannot escape accountability at the hands of the Congress party because we are the guardians and protectors of the Constitution. Safeguarding the Constitution is our duty,” he said.“Let me assure all Congress workers: PM Narendra Modi, Amit Shah and Gyanesh Kumar will face justice and will pay the price for what they have done.”Taking a swipe at the Prime Minister, Gandhi asked, “Where has his 56-inch chest gone? Perhaps you haven’t noticed, but have you seen Modi ji’s face lately? Where has his 56-inch chest gone? These days, Modi ji cannot even stand before us. He and Amit Shah know that the Congress party has taken them on and cornered them."Turning to student protests in Delhi, Gandhi said, “Look at what is happening in Delhi today. Pellet guns are being fired at students because they are raising concerns about vote theft, employment and the rising cost of education.”In Goa, Gandhi alleged widespread corruption, saying the state had been turned into a “model” for corruption. He urged voters to back the Congress, citing concerns over land conversion, alleged land grabbing, unemployment and the daily humiliation faced by residents.“The injustices you are suffering, the humiliation you face every day, and the way your land is being taken away from you and sold off — if you want to put a stop to all this, you must give the Congress party a full majority,” he said.Gandhi joined the Congress’s ‘Goy Rakhon Yatra’ in Margao, walking around two kilometres with party workers and leaders. The 27-day campaign, which began on September 22 and covered all 40 Assembly constituencies, concluded on Sunday.The Congress has positioned the yatra as a campaign to safeguard Goa’s land, environment, cultural heritage and identity.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, Iowa road projects used plastic additive equal to 15 million bottles; on one busy test stretch, it held up better than adjacent regular asphalt
articles.summary: Explore how Iowa's incorporation of recycled plastic in asphalt projects, equivalent to 15 million bottles, is promising better road durability and sustainability.
articles.body: Despite its rather unremarkable appearance, asphalt is a substance that is difficult to enhance. It is cracked by frigid winters, rutted by heavy trucks, and the budget of a road agency is depleted with each pothole repair. According to OECD data used in a 2025 Iowa State University study, only roughly 9% of plastic garbage is successfully recycled, indicating that the globe has its own plastic problem. Some engineers think that by incorporating recycled plastic into the road itself, both problems might be resolved simultaneously. In the Des Moines area, Iowa has been attempting precisely that, and preliminary results from one test stretch are promising.The additive, called NewRoad, is developed by NVI Advanced Materials Group of Florida, which characterises it as a designed polymer derived from recycled industrial and post-consumer plastic. Some 300,000 pounds of it went into road projects throughout the Des Moines area in 2021, about the same as 15 million water bottles. On the oldest test length, a heavily utilised segment of Northeast 22nd Street, Iowa Department of Transportation workers claimed the plastic section was holding up better than the traditional asphalt beside it.What went into the roadThe first Des Moines-area trial began in 2016, after Construction Material Testing president Doug Clement approached the Iowa Department of Transportation about using NewRoad. The initial test used a polystyrene-based additive in about 500 U.S. tons of asphalt mix placed on sections of Northeast 22nd Street. This was a small field trial on an active road, separate from the broader use of the additive across metro-area projects in later years.Separately, more than 300,000 pounds of NewRoad additive were used across Des Moines-area road projects in 2021, equivalent to about 136 metric tonnes of the product. Axios Des Moines reported that this regional total was equivalent to 15 million water bottles. The figure refers to the additive used across multiple projects, not to the total weight of asphalt on the original 2016 test stretch or to 300,000 pounds of pure plastic in that one road.The company believes its polymers reinforce the asphalt mix and help reduce rutting, moisture damage and cracking. Its website says it can deliver up to 50 per cent longer pavement life and up to 50 per cent less rutting in a Hamburg test, a lab test where a loaded wheel rolls over a wet asphalt sample again and again. These are the manufacturer's data, not independently obtained figures. The real question is, what happened to the plastic under traffic?Progress on the test stretchThe strongest public evidence so far comes from preliminary observations by Iowa DOT staff. In a January 2022 report, Axios Des Moines quoted construction technician Matt Miller saying that a heavily trafficked section near the Polk County Jail was holding up better than an adjacent section made with conventional asphalt. The report also quoted field technician Shane Fetters, who said a comparison made more than five years after installation showed less rutting and cracking in the treated section. These were field observations, not a published long-term engineering evaluation.A separate laboratory study offers a note of caution. Iowa State University researchers tested recycled plastics in asphalt and concrete for the Minnesota Department of Transportation, and their final report was published in August 2025. The study found that an asphalt mixture made by adding post-consumer recycled plastic to the binder through a wet process had lower cracking resistance than an otherwise identical mixture without plastic, according to the published report. The researchers also reported that some plastic separated from the modified binder and raised concerns about variation in plastic quality and long-term durability. The study tested specific laboratory mixtures for Minnesota, not the NewRoad sections in Des Moines. Its findings therefore do not directly confirm or disprove the Iowa DOT staff’s roadside observations; they show that results depend on the plastic, blending method and asphalt mix design.The Next stepsThe Iowa DOT isn't planning to stop with visual impressions. The department aims to remove sections of the road that employed the plastic mix and the standard asphalt, and then compare how each is holding up, WOI said. Testing samples from the treated and conventional asphalt sections side by side could provide stronger evidence of differences in cracking, rutting and overall pavement condition. The research portion of the Iowa State paper finds a similar conclusion. It also calls for wide-scale field experiments and long-term performance monitoring while highlighting the other promise of the plastic: less landfill trash and lower carbon emissions.Iowa is also considering plastic beyond the road surface. In October 2021, the Iowa Highway Research Board approved a $349,960 Iowa State University project to evaluate recycled plastics, including material from defunct wind turbine blades, as a method to improve the base of gravel roadways. It also includes pilot test parts on actual roads.For anyone following this story, the short version is easy. Iowa has been adding a recycled plastic additive to asphalt on an increasing number of Des Moines area roadways, including an earlier test stretch on Northeast 22nd Street, where state transportation staff reported less rutting and cracking than on adjacent conventional asphalt. The research is promising but early, based on only preliminary DOT observations and corporate data. Independent lab testing suggests results depend on how the plastic is added. The cut-out comparison planned by the DOT should provide the clearest answer yet.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: France's unrest spills across borders as protests turn violent in Belgium, Italy
articles.summary: Violent protests over rising living costs and public services spread beyond France into neighbouring Belgium and Italy on Saturday.
articles.body: Violent protests over rising living costs and public services spread beyond France into neighbouring Belgium and Italy on Saturday. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse crowds as demonstrators clashed with security forces, looted shops and set property on fire. The unrest in France left one demonstrator dead, injured more than 500 police officers and led to nearly 1,800 arrests, according to the interior minister.In Belgium, clashes broke out between protesters and police in Brussels and Liège. In Italy, violence erupted in central Milan, where masked demonstrators threw stones and paving blocks at riot police, set fire to barricades and damaged property. The unrest came as France grappled with one of its most violent days of demonstrations in years, driven by anger over rising prices, school conditions and declining public services.Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin condemned the violence in Brussels, describing it as an organised attempt to destabilise society. He said federal police were supporting local forces and warned that all necessary measures would be taken to restore order.“NO, what is unfolding in Brussels is no longer mere protest! It is pure and simple violence, organised and repeated to destabilise our society. The federal police are in support of the local police. All necessary means will be used to restore order in the face of the rioters,” Quintin posted on X.In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also condemned the violence after demonstrations in Milan descended into clashes, detentions and property destruction. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds, while at least two officers were injured and around 50 demonstrators, including several minors, were detained, news agency LaPresse reported.The violence forced police to clear Milan's Piazza del Duomo and a luxury shopping arcade, areas that would usually be crowded with shoppers. The march, organised against wars and rising living costs, had begun peacefully before masked protesters attacked police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables. Images from the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri vehicle.“Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni wrote on social media, criticising “hooligans who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and hold entire cities hostage.”Milan's centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, acknowledged the concerns behind the demonstrations but condemned the destruction. “The reasons for the protests were understandable. The violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable,” he said.Meloni also drew a distinction between peaceful protesters and those involved in violence during nationwide rallies. “I have great respect for the thousands of people who today demonstrated peacefully, including those who took part in the mobilisation called by the CGIL, which also saw the participation of left-wing leaders,” she said. “Whatever the ideas for which one demonstrates, participation is the foundation of any healthy democracy.”France faces mounting pressure after deadly unrestFrance remained at the centre of the unrest on Sunday as authorities began assessing damage across the country following Saturday's demonstrations. The protests brought together more than half a million people in cities nationwide, with peaceful marches giving way to violence in several locations.One demonstrator died after suffering a cardiac arrest during protests in Paris. Police arrested around 1,800 people across France, including a record 855 in the capital, while more than 500 officers were injured, the interior minister said.Violent groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. A town hall in Limoges, a building that is 143 years old, was partially destroyed in an arson attack. In Bordeaux, a masked mob entered the residence of the local prefect, while the city's mayor, Thomas Cazenave, said up to 100 shops had been looted.A large clean-up operation began in cities across France, including Lille, Marseille, Strasbourg and Bordeaux. In Paris, smashed shop windows, burnt-out bicycles and graffiti marked areas where demonstrations had turned violent.The protests initially emerged last month over poor school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs. They later expanded into a wider movement against inequality, public spending cuts, rising fuel prices and the declining purchasing power of households.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 550,000 people had taken part in the demonstrations, including 110,000 in Paris. He said police had made 400 arrests over vandalism charges, while subsequent nationwide figures put the total number detained at nearly 1,800.President Emmanuel Macron vowed action against those responsible for violence and looting, while defending the right to peaceful protest.“No room for violence in our Republic. Those who have ransacked, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished,” Macron wrote on X. “To the law enforcement forces, guarantors of the right to demonstrate, I express the support of the Nation. We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who seek only to bring down our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so.”Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be intimidated by violence, blaming the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals. Economy Minister Roland Lescure promised support for businesses affected by the destruction and said those responsible would be held accountable.“Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos,” Lescure said.The unrest has added to pressure on Macron and his government ahead of next year's presidential election. Former figures from France's Yellow Vest movement are also expected to join demonstrations in support of high-school students, French media reported.The Yellow Vest movement began in 2018 in response to rising fuel prices and economic inequality. Its demonstrations drew thousands onto the streets and were marked by violent clashes with police. More than 2,500 protesters and 1,800 police personnel were injured in those confrontations.The latest demonstrations have once again exposed the challenge facing European governments as public anger over living costs and public services intersects with wider political grievances. While many people have taken to the streets peacefully, violence in France, Belgium and Italy has prompted authorities to warn against attacks on police, public institutions and businesses.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2024, sisters Susan and Marianne Fowler protected 36 more Tennessee acres after their uncle died, keeping a promise to their aunt as developers bought nearby land
articles.summary: Susan and Marianne Fowler emphasize conservation by preserving their family farm in East Tennessee. In 2024, they added 36 acres of protected land, fulfilling a promise to their aunt as housing developments encroach on historic farmlands.
articles.body: The same scene keeps repeating as you drive through East Tennessee's valleys. After a century of hay production, a field receives a survey flag, a sign and finally a row of new homes. As more people relocate to the state and buyers seek out open land to build on, land that has been in one family for many generations is discreetly changing hands, and the pace has accelerated. A modest deed of the opposite kind stands out against that background since it was intentional and planned to remain forever. Regardless of what happens to the surrounding area, two sisters in Anderson County resolved that the farm where their father was born should remain a farm.In 2024, Susan and Marianne Fowler conserved an additional 36 acres of the farm with support from the charity Land Trust for Tennessee. The new acreage adds to the 56 acres of ancient farmland they had already preserved on the property in 2010. Their promise to their aunt, along with the sight of nearby property being bought up for development, motivated them to protect the additional acreage.A promise to protect the farmThe land has been in the Fowler family since 1900. Susan Fowler says her father was born and raised in the house, which her uncle later occupied. After her uncle died, his wife and Susan's sister Marianne became increasingly concerned about development in the area.In 2010, while their aunt was still alive, the sisters placed the first 56 acres under a conservation easement. They promised their aunt they would protect the adjacent acreage as well. In 2024, they fulfilled that promise by placing another 36 acres under an easement. Susan Fowler described the landscape this way: “This is a beautiful valley, and some of it needs to be maintained the way it was to begin with.”The new protected property is located in the north central portion of Anderson County, in the Dutch Valley on the east valley floor of Walden Ridge. It is a piece of East Tennessee that has been moulded by the North Cumberland Mountains, the Clinch River and Norris Lake. But the most important feature is not on a map. It’s the legal documents that protect the land long after the people who signed them are gone.How does a conservation easement workA conservation easement is a legal, binding contract in which the landowner voluntarily limits the use or development of his land in perpetuity. The LTTN notes that land with an easement is still private property and can be sold or left to heirs, but the easement goes with the land no matter who owns it next. That’s the difference between this arrangement and just selling or giving away land.Each easement is customised. Owners can keep rights to farm, cut timber, hunt or build a future house, though some things may require clearance from the land trust first. An easement does not necessarily mean the land is open to the public. It can also be partial and phased, as the Fowler farm was protected, initially in 2010 and then in 2024.Once the documents are signed, the land trust gets to work. It checks in annually with the landowner on each protected site to ensure the terms are being met, and these visits are especially important when ownership changes. The entire procedure takes an average of six to nine months from initial contact to recorded easement. The trust is free but landowners pay for their own advisors such as lawyers and surveyors. Owners may also be eligible for a federal income tax deduction for the decline in the appraised value of the land, the trust says, and recommends they consult a legal or tax specialist first.Why Tennessee's farming is under threatLTTN says it has helped protect more than 137,000 acres in 76 Tennessee counties over more than 25 years. But the loss on the other side of the ledger is substantial.A University of Tennessee analysis cited by American Farmland Trust estimates that Tennessee converted about 1.1 million acres of farmland to other uses between 1997 and 2017 and another 430,000 acres between 2017 and 2023. Spread across six full years, the latter figure averages about 8.2 acres per hour. With Tennessee's average farm size at 170 acres, that is equivalent to roughly one average-sized farm every 21 hours.The American Farmland Trust forecasts that between 2016 and 2040, Tennessee will lose more than one million acres of farmland, the third-highest loss in the nation. It also defines conservation easements owned by land trusts as a voluntary tool for farmers to limit development rights while retaining ownership and continuing to farm.The 36 acres protected in 2024 add to the 56 acres the Fowler sisters placed under conservation easement in 2010. The sisters still own the property, but the permanent easement held by The Land Trust for Tennessee restricts future development under the agreement's terms. Those restrictions remain in effect even if ownership changes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A former precision-tool factory sat abandoned for years before a $43.7 million redevelopment turned it into a solar-powered community hub in New York
articles.summary: A former precision-tool factory in Poughkeepsie, New York, spent years standing unused before a $43.7 million redevelopment gave the ageing industrial
articles.body: A former precision-tool factory in Poughkeepsie, New York, spent years standing unused before a $43.7 million redevelopment gave the ageing industrial site a new purpose. The property, once home to the Standard Gage factory, has been transformed into the Northside Hub, a solar-powered campus combining offices, community facilities and public green space. Environmental nonprofit Scenic Hudson led the five-year project, which retains the site's industrial history while introducing rooftop gardens, solar panels and areas for local gatherings. More than a headquarters, the development opens part of the former factory site to businesses, community organisations and residents, bringing new activity to a long-neglected property.Northside Hub transforms the former Standard Gage factory in PoughkeepsieThe Northside Hub occupies the former Standard Gage factory, a 20th-century manufacturing property in the north of Poughkeepsie. Like other industrial buildings in older American cities, the site had reached a point where its condition made its future uncertain. Its ageing structures and brownfield setting presented challenges, but the property also offered an opportunity to reuse land that had already been developed rather than expand into undeveloped areas.Scenic Hudson, the Poughkeepsie-based environmental organisation behind the project, took on the task of bringing the property back into use. The redevelopment unfolded over five years, with a reported investment of $43.7 million, as reported by WAMC Northeast Public Radio. The intention was to create a permanent base for the nonprofit while making the wider site useful to the surrounding community.The approach reflects a practical question facing cities with a long industrial history: what should happen to factories and commercial buildings once their original purpose has disappeared? Leaving them unused can allow deterioration to continue, while demolishing them and starting again can mean losing existing structures and consuming additional resources. At the Northside Hub, the decision was to adapt the site for a mixture of work, public activities and outdoor use.Northside Hub combines community facilities with rooftop gardensScenic Hudson's offices occupy part of the renovated complex, but the building has not been designed exclusively for its employees. More than one-third of the Northside Hub is intended for lease to businesses and community organisations, giving other groups a place to work and hold activities.Inside, the facilities include an auditorium, meeting rooms, office accommodation and spaces available for rental. These areas can serve different purposes throughout the week, from organisational meetings to larger gatherings and community events.The outdoor areas are another part of the development. A park and pavilion provide places for people to meet, while the building's rooftop includes planted areas overlooking Fall Kill Creek. The landscaping incorporates native grasses and sedum, plants suited to the roof environment and capable of helping manage rainwater.The site began welcoming the public through a community block party held on 10 October 2025. Families, children and local organisations attended, with activities taking place around the new park and pavilion. Scenic Hudson staff had moved into the headquarters in September that year, and the organisation planned for the campus to open permanently to the public in January 2026.Solar panels and green design shape the net-zero campusEnergy generation is built into the Northside Hub's design. Solar panels sit on the roof and above sections of the car park, where timber canopies support the installations and provide shade for vehicles. The arrangement allows the project to use both the building and its surrounding paved areas to generate electricity.The organisation describes the campus as a net-zero development. Its renewable energy system forms part of a wider design that incorporates planted roofing, outdoor green space and stormwater management. The roof vegetation helps absorb and manage rainfall, reducing the amount of water that runs directly off the building.These features give the project an environmental role beyond its use as an office complex. The redevelopment brings a previously developed property back into service while incorporating energy generation and landscaping into the site. Its value, however, rests on more than the installation of solar panels. The building also has to accommodate daily work, community use and the upkeep of its public areas.The combination of solar infrastructure and shared facilities makes the Northside Hub an example of how an older industrial property can be adapted to meet several needs at once. Its design does not depend on turning the site into a conventional office building or a park alone.An approach shaped by Poughkeepsie's industrial historyScenic Hudson has spent decades working to protect the Hudson Valley's landscapes and outdoor spaces. Reusing an industrial site in Poughkeepsie offers a way to apply that environmental outlook within an established urban area, where vacant buildings and previously developed land can present alternatives to building on undeveloped ground.The Northside Hub's principal architect, Justin Brown, has pointed to the potential of ageing industrial buildings in smaller post-industrial American cities. Such properties can be difficult to restore, particularly when roofs and other parts of the structure have deteriorated. Yet their existing buildings and locations may still offer opportunities for new uses.The Standard Gage factory provided that starting point. Instead of treating the property solely as a problem to be cleared, the redevelopment made its existing industrial character part of a new campus. The project also creates space for organisations beyond Scenic Hudson, allowing the site to function as a local resource as well as an administrative base.How an old factory found a new role in the cityThe Northside Hub brings several functions together on land that had previously stood underused. Its offices provide a home for Scenic Hudson, its rentable areas offer space for other organisations, and its park, pavilion and rooftop planting introduce public and environmental features into the former industrial property. For Poughkeepsie, the redevelopment also gives a historic factory a continuing place in the city rather than leaving it as a remnant of an earlier manufacturing era. The building's new role is different from the one for which it was constructed, but the site remains in use and has been adapted to support a range of activities.The project does not remove every challenge associated with redeveloping an old industrial property. It does, however, demonstrate what can be achieved when rehabilitation, renewable energy and community facilities are planned as parts of the same development. The former Standard Gage factory now serves as a workplace and gathering place, with its solar-powered systems and planted outdoor areas integrated into the wider site.For Scenic Hudson, the Northside Hub is both a headquarters and a working example of its approach to the built environment: making use of existing urban land while creating room for people and nature.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2001, Tony Bennett and Susan Benedetto helped open a public arts school for 250 students; 25 years later, it offers young New Yorkers a 750-seat concert hall, dance studios and a film lab
articles.summary: In 2001, late singer and painter Tony Bennett and his wife, Susan Benedetto, helped open a public high school in New York for students who wanted to
articles.body: In 2001, late singer and painter Tony Bennett and his wife, Susan Benedetto, helped open a public high school in New York for students who wanted to pursue the arts alongside their academic studies. It began in temporary quarters with space for 250 students. Twenty-five years later, the Frank Sinatra School of the Arts in Astoria, Queens, has specialist studios, theatres, a film lab and a concert hall where students can perform and screen their work. The school was named after Frank Sinatra, Bennett’s friend and fellow singer. According to the school’s official website, the idea began in 1999, when Bennett and Benedetto, a former public school teacher, set out to create a public high school that combined serious arts training with a strong academic curriculum.They worked with the New York City Department of Education and local leaders to bring the plan to life. The school opened in temporary premises in 2001 before moving to its permanent building at the Kaufman Astoria Studios complex in 2009.From temporary classrooms to a purpose-built arts schoolThe move to the permanent building gave students access to dedicated spaces for different art forms. The school’s facilities include two dance studios, two black-box theatres, two fine-art studios, a stagecraft workshop, an art gallery, choral and orchestral studios, private practice rooms and a film lab. It also has an outdoor rooftop performance space. The building was designed to give high school students the opportunity to learn and perform in facilities suited to professional arts production. Its concert hall hosts school musicals, instrumental and vocal performances, dance shows and screenings of films made by students.The venue is named the Tony Bennett Concert Hall. As per the school’s website, it as an 800-seat venue. The permanent school building was designed by architect Susan T. Rodriguez of Ennead Architects. It opened in 2009 after a capital campaign helped fund its construction.Students study six arts disciplinesThe Frank Sinatra School of the Arts is a public high school where students audition for admission and choose a specialisation. According to Exploring the Arts, they can major in dance, drama, film, fine art, vocal music or instrumental music. Arts training is combined with academic subjects. The school’s mission statement says students follow a four-year curriculum designed to prepare them for competitive colleges and conservatories.Why Tony Bennett and Susan Benedetto started the schoolThe project was part of Bennett and Benedetto’s wider effort to expand access to arts education in public schools. They also established Exploring the Arts, which supports arts programmes and provides opportunities such as internships and scholarships. As reported by local news outlet QNS, Benedetto spoke about what the school meant to the couple after Bennett’s death. “Tony was so proud of the Frank Sinatra School, proud of the hardworking teachers and school leaders and so very proud of the school’s talented students,” she said. “Because of Tony, these young people have committed themselves to craft and a lifelong pursuit of learning.” Benedetto had worked as a public school teacher before co-founding the school. Her experience in education, combined with Bennett’s career in music and painting, shaped their plan to create a school where students could develop artistic skills without giving up a broad academic education.When asked why the school was named after Sinatra rather than himself, Bennett pointed to his close friendship with the singer. The name was intended as a tribute to the man he considered his best friend and colleague.A school that continues to carry their visionThe school continues to receive support from Exploring the Arts, which was founded to help sustain its arts programmes and expand opportunities for students. The organisation has since extended its work to public high schools in New York City and Los Angeles. What started as a public high school in temporary quarters now combines academic study with dedicated spaces for dance, theatre, film, visual art and music. Its history reflects Bennett and Benedetto’s stated aim: to make arts education part of public schooling rather than something students must find outside it.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Michigan family owned a one-third-acre lakefront cottage before Prairie View Park was built; more than 60 years later, courts say Kalamazoo County can condemn it
articles.summary: A long-running legal dispute over a one-third-acre lakefront property surrounded by a public park has reached a key stage.
articles.body: A long-running legal dispute over a one-third-acre lakefront property surrounded by a public park has reached a key stage. A state appeals court has ruled that local officials can take the land using their legal powers to acquire private property. The Michigan Court of Appeals upheld a lower court ruling that allows Kalamazoo County to take ownership of the residential cottage at 1739 East U Avenue in Vicksburg. The property sits on the shore of Gourdneck Lake and is completely surrounded by Prairie View County Park. According to court records in case number 367503, County of Kalamazoo v James Berry, a three-judge panel upheld the lower court's decision. The panel included Presiding Judge Elizabeth L. Wallace, Judge Thomas C. Cameron and Judge Sima G. Korobkin. The judges found that county officials had met the legal requirements set out in Michigan's Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act. The ruling allows county officials to move ahead with adding the privately owned plot to the surrounding park. It also brings a property dispute that has lasted for decades closer to a resolution.Six decades of park expansion and property disputesThe dispute began with the creation of Prairie View Park in 1960. Before county officials started buying land for the recreational area, a private family had already bought the lakefront cottage and the land around it. As the county acquired nearby properties to build public facilities, picnic shelters and swimming areas, the one-third-acre plot with the cottage remained in private hands. For more than sixty years, family descendants continued to own the cottage, even though public land surrounded it on all sides. Tensions grew when county officials tried to acquire the property to complete the park. In court filings, county officials described the cottage plot as a "landlocked parcel" within the park's boundaries. They argued that acquiring it was necessary to complete public recreation plans first developed when the park project began in 1960. When talks failed to produce a voluntary sale, Kalamazoo County began formal legal proceedings to take the property under state eminent domain laws. These laws allow the government to acquire private land for an approved public purpose.Legal requirements and challenges over public purposeIn their appeal against the trial court's order allowing the county to take the property, the owners argued that county officials had no legal authority to do so and had failed to prove that the taking served a genuine public purpose. Lawyers for the family argued that local officials could not use a development plan created 60 years ago to justify taking private land today. Citing earlier state court decisions, the family's lawyers said that more than six decades had passed, making the original public purpose outdated. The Court of Appeals rejected these arguments. In an opinion issued on behalf of the full panel, the judges ruled that adding private land directly to an existing public park clearly qualifies as a public use under state law. "A public park is clearly a public-purpose use of real property," the judges wrote. They referred to section 123.61 of the Michigan Compiled Laws, which specifically allows local governments to acquire land for park expansion through condemnation. In response to the family's argument about the long delay, the judges stated: "This argument is unconvincing because plaintiff intends to presently incorporate the subject property into the park." The court also found that Kalamazoo County had followed all the required legal steps under Michigan's eminent domain laws. It confirmed that the trial court had the legal authority to hear and decide the condemnation case.Defense arguments and remaining legal optionsThroughout the case, lawyers for the family argued that the county's actions unnecessarily interfered with long-standing private property rights. Lawyers from Levine & Levine, who represent members of the Berry family, had previously described the dispute in public statements and court filings as an excessive use of government power. They argued that county officials had not shown an urgent public need to take the cottage. The family's lawyers also questioned the procedures followed during county meetings. In separate court filings, they alleged that local commissioners had violated open meetings laws while discussing the property. Although the appeals court ruling confirms that the county can legally claim a public purpose for taking the land, Michigan's Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act requires the government to pay property owners fair compensation. If the two sides cannot agree on the property's fair market value, the case will return to the trial court to determine how much money the county must pay the family. articles.title: Florida has completed a $191.8 million water-reclamation project, St. Johns County's largest ever, built to treat 3.25 million gallons a day and keep 1 million pounds of nutrients from the Matanzas River
articles.summary: St. Johns County Utilities officials have gathered to celebrate the completion of the State Road 207 Water Reclamation Facility.
articles.body: St. Johns County Utilities officials have gathered to celebrate the completion of the State Road 207 Water Reclamation Facility. The $191.8 million project is the largest capital improvement project in the county's history. Located at 3055 State Road 207 in Elkton, the new plant treats wastewater and turns it into reclaimed water that is not safe for drinking but can be used for purposes such as watering lawns and landscapes. By supplying treated wastewater for irrigation, county officials hope to reduce the area's dependence on the Floridan Aquifer, Northeast Florida's main source of fresh drinking water. The project comes at an important time for the region, as local officials continue to monitor drought conditions. According to announcements from St. Johns County Utilities, the St. Johns River Water Management District's Phase III Extreme Water Shortage Order remains in effect. The order follows a shortage of rainfall across the region, with rainfall levels earlier this year measuring more than eight inches below the 12-month average.Capacity and environmental performanceThe facility began operational testing on May 11 and has an initial treatment capacity of 3.25 million gallons per day. St. Johns County design documents show that the plant was built so its capacity can be expanded in stages. As local demand grows, the facility can increase its daily treatment capacity to 6.5 million gallons. The plant is also designed to meet environmental requirements under Florida Senate Bill 64. This law requires the state to end treated wastewater discharges into surface waters when those discharges do not provide a useful benefit. County estimates show that over the next 20 years, the facility will prevent more than one million pounds of nutrient pollution, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, from entering the Matanzas River. Alan Flood, Senior Engineer for the St. Johns County Utility Department, explained how the facility will help protect local water supplies over time. “This project allows us to substitute a slightly lower quality of water for irrigation, extending the useful life of our aquifer for many years,” Flood said. In a separate statement released through the county's public communications, Flood added: “This facility represents a transformative investment in St. Johns County's future.”Engineering and system integrationThe $191.8 million facility was built under a progressive design-build contract with Jacobs, an international professional services firm that specialises in engineering and infrastructure. Under this type of contract, design and construction work can take place at the same time, helping speed up the project. Connecting the new plant to the county's existing utility network also required major construction outside the facility itself. The work included: Installing approximately 15 miles of large wastewater and reclaimed water transmission pipes. Building a new main wastewater pumping station. Building a separate reclaimed water booster pumping station to maintain water pressure throughout the distribution network.Financial structure and municipal operationsThe St. Johns County Utilities Department managed funding for the project through an enterprise fund. Under this system, utility service charges and connection fees pay for operating costs and major investments, rather than general property taxes. County records state that average monthly residential utility bills in St. Johns County remain approximately 10 per cent below the regional average. The completed facility adds a major part to St. Johns County's water infrastructure. It gives regional planners a more sustainable way to manage wastewater while helping protect local rivers and underground water reserves.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data centre operated by technology company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.Russia’s ministry of defence said its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones across 15 Russian regions, the annexed Crimean peninsula and the Black Sea.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS that Kyiv was “resisting” Moscow’s invasion but could not “change the current course of events.”Meanwhile, a woman was killed and at least two people, including a six-year-old girl, were injured in two strikes on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials told news agency AP. Regional military administration head Mykhailo Semikin said two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged.Zelenskyy alleges 76 attacks on energy sectorEarlier, Zelenskyy said Russia had continued targeting energy infrastructure despite Trump’s announcement on October 11 that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”.“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times,” Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that attacks overnight had hit energy facilities in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi and Odesa regions.He said tens of thousands of families remained without power and accused Moscow of attempting to cause a blackout.“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting,” Zelenskyy wrote.“It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps,” he added.Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign ministry also expressed regret over Ukrainian drones entering Lithuanian airspace, saying the incident may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare.“We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X. articles.title: Akola Farmer Alleges Microfinance Recovery Pressure, Wife’s Photos Clicked
articles.summary: Akola farmer alleges microfinance firm pressured loan recovery despite govt drought directives, with repeated visits and wife’s photos taken without consent.
articles.body: Akola: A farmer from Dongargaon in Akola district has accused a microfinance company of piling on pressure to repay a loan in violation of govt’s directives in times of drought. The aggrieved farmer, Yogesh Nagapure, alleged company representatives repeatedly visit their house and took photographs of his wife without her consent.“We repaid ₹30,000 of the ₹50,000 loan and are ready to pay the outstanding amount too. But our crop has been damaged, and farming has not generated adequate income. They took my wife’s photograph without telling us why it was being taken or how it would be used,” Nagapure alleged.The allegations surfaced days after chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule directed banks to consider the financial distress of farmers affected by crop losses. During his visit to Yevata in Akola district on October 3, Bawankule specifically directed lending institutions against forceful loan recovery.When contacted, company representatives reportedly said they had not received any order in this regard and suggested their head office might provide more information. The company’s detailed response to the allegations is awaited.Ravi Kant Upkar, head of the Krantikari Shetkari Sanghatana, alleged that the govt has failed to curb coercive loan recovery practices by microfinance firms, leaving farmers under mounting financial stress.“There is no visible control over the arbitrary functioning of these microfinance companies. The govt is making announcements, but the ground reality is different. We stand firmly with the farmers,” Upkar said.Agricultural expert Dr Nilesh Patil said gaps in the availability, timing and duration of formal agricultural loans continue to push farmers towards alternative lenders, despite presence of public-sector banks, cooperative banks and other institutional lending networks.“Farmers often have to arrange funds within a limited period, from June to March, while repayment depends heavily on performance of crops, which is vulnerable to vagaries of nature and other risks. articles.title: Chennai gets a weekend rain trailer
articles.summary: Chennai sees 10.5cm weekend rain; GCC clears 35 roads and 16 subways, but north Chennai and Velachery flood amid clogged canals and incomplete drains.
articles.body: Chennai: The city got a preview of what the monsoon could bring, with 10.5cm of rain falling over 24 hours, ending at 6am on Sunday. The first spell exposed uneven flood preparedness. Overnight operations by more than 15,000 Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) staff cleared 35 waterlogged roads and 16 subways, but parts of north Chennai and Velachery remained flooded because of clogged canals, incomplete drains and stalled work.GCC data showed Parry’s got 36.3cm of rain, Ennore Kathivakkam 34cm, Meenambakkam 28cm and Central 27.4cm. Velachery, which got 2cm, still saw knee-deep water in streets at Bhuvaneswari Nagar, Ram Nagar, AGS Colony and Tansi Nagar. Water receded within hours as pumps were deployed.Geetha Ganesh, secretary of the AGS Colony Residents’ Welfare Association, said water rose to 1ft in some areas. “Most drains here carry water towards Veerangal Odai, which is clogged with garbage and silt. Of the 3.8km-long canal, around 1.5km has been desilted,” she said. Residents flagged encroachments near six vent culverts around Vijayanagar bus terminus and Perungudi railway station.In north Chennai, Prakasham Salai in Broadway and Vyasarpadi Jeeva were among the worst-affected areas. At Vyasarpadi, a flyover project that was due for completion nearly a year ago remains unfinished, along with a drain channel to Otteri Nullah and collection wells meant to prevent subway flooding.GCC commissioner G S Sameeran inspected Prakasham Salai, while municipal administration and water supply secretary Gagandeep Singh Bedi visited Vyasarpadi Jeeva. Chief minister C Joseph Vijay later reviewed preparedness at the GCC control room and told officials to track weather updates and keep flood response ready.Of 21 locations that recorded very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall, 14 were in north Chennai. T K Shanmugam, president of the Federation of North Chennai Residents’ Welfare Association, said, “The desilting and flood-mitigation work began a few months before the northeast monsoon last year, when there was insufficient machinery to complete them. The work was eventually stalled once the rains began.”In Pattalam, resident Ramaboopathy said a 24km stormwater drain built in 2024 was not connected to nearby channels. articles.title: Farakka Barrage theme turns Patna pandal into water debate
articles.summary: Patna Durga Puja pandal recreates Farakka Barrage with working water feature, spotlighting Bihar’s flood, erosion and displacement concerns amid treaty talks.
articles.body: Patna: A Durga Puja pandal in Patna has turned the contentious Farakka water-sharing issue into a striking visual statement, recreating the barrage while depicting Bihar’s floods, riverbank erosion and displacement.At Kasturba Path in the Jamuna Apartment lane off Boring Road, the Shri Shri Sarvajan Durga Puja Committee has built a 55-foot-high and 55-foot-wide replica of the Farakka Barrage, complete with gates and a working water system that sends streams cascading through the structure.The lower portion portrays the human cost of floods — families forced from their homes, people carrying belongings on their heads, submerged houses and farmland, and riverbank erosion. Messages around the structure include “Our water, our right” and a call to reconsider the Farakka water-sharing arrangement.“Every year we say Bihar is drowning, but we believe the larger issue is India’s water management. Bihar is caught between water released from Nepal upstream and the water-management arrangements downstream,” said Raju Yadav, vice-president of the puja committee.The committee has highlighted silt accumulation, changes in the river’s flow, flooding, erosion and drainage concerns. The theme comes as the 1996 India-Bangladesh Ganga water-sharing treaty completes its 30-year term in Dec 2026. The agreement governs the sharing of Ganga waters at Farakka during the dry season.The issue has also become a political talking point in Bihar. JD(U) national working president and Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Kumar Jha has demanded that any future arrangement take Bihar’s water requirements into account, including its needs up to 2050.Jha visited the pandal on Saturday and appreciated the initiative. The organisers said he assured them he would take up the issue.“We cannot go everywhere and protest. Through the media and this pandal, we want to spread the message across Patna, Bihar and the country,” Yadav said.The working water feature is among the main attractions. Motors and a fountain mechanism recreate the flow through the barrage with the water flow increasing when the four model gates are opened.“It is a small space, but we have tried to show what happens around the barrage. When the gates open, the water flow increases. We wanted people to see the issue rather than just read about it,” Yadav said.The pandal was constructed over about 42-43 days by artisans from Kolkata and West Bengal. Around 10-12 local committee members were involved. articles.summary: Durga Puja pandals across Mumbai Metropolitan Region drew big weekend crowds, with themes, bhog, cultural shows and performances in Vashi, Thane, Nerul and Vasai.
articles.body: Mumbai: The Bengali community across Mumbai Metropolitan Region spent a leisurely Sunday visiting Durga Puja pandals to savour bhog lunch and stayed back for the evening entertainment shows.Vashi Cultural Association is celebrating its 22nd Durgotsav in an 80,000 sq ft pandal at ICL School Ground, Sector 15. Performers include singers Amit Kumar, Javed Ali, Rupankar Bagchi and Jayati Chakraborty. A fashion show, dhunuchi competition and mukt manch are on schedule, said organiser Ashim Dey.The theme of the five-year-old NRI Seawoods ‘gharowa’ style Pujo is ‘Gram Bangla: Back to Roots’. Spokesman Soumyajit Niyogi said, “Our rustic pandal is crafted with traditional material. The unveiling of Ma Durga’s idol was performed by children from Jeevan Jyoti Ashram, a Nerul orphanage.”At Sector 8 in Sanpada, Bengali Cultural Association secretary Buddhadev Karmakar said, “Our Gram Bangla theme is in a temple-shaped pandal. Since Durga Puja has an additional day, we have five days of cultural soirees. Omkar Band from Kolkata will perform on Ashtami and singers Swakshar Basu and Rahul Joshi on Navami.”In Thane, the theme of the 24th Aamra Prabashi Sharodotsav at TMC Ground, Hiranandani Estate, is ‘Kolkatar Pothe Pothe’. It recreates the sights, sounds and memories of Kolkata through an experiential mandap and audio-visual trip of architecture and streetscape. The venue spans 1,60,000 sq ft, said president Arnab De. Anjali, dhak, bhog, music, food and adda are drawing devotees.The older namesake, Aamra Prabasi Nerul Durga Utsav (Ramleela Maidan), is in its 34th year. “Our festivities are inspired by the theme of Adi Yoga, while preserving Bengal’s heritage through a traditional Sabeki idol and a pandal designed like a Bengali village,” said chairperson Sushanta Saha. It brings 300 families to celebrate in a homely way, said president Subrata Mitra.In Vasai, Bassein Bengal Club is hosting its 42nd Durga Puja at its Kali Mandir. articles.title: Pakistani forces kill 8 militants in Balochistan, raid hideouts as abductions rise
articles.summary: Pakistani security forces on Sunday reportedly killed eight militants in three intelligence-led operations across districts of Balochistan province, amid
articles.body: Pakistani security forces on Sunday reportedly killed eight militants in three intelligence-led operations across districts of Balochistan province, amid rising cases of abduction in the troubled region.The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas, according to the Inter Service Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of the Pakistan Army.In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists trying to set up a roadblock to disrupt local traffic were "intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five terrorists", the ISPR said in a statement.In Nushki district, security forces stormed a hideout, and two terrorists were killed in an intense exchange of fire, the army said. Around 500 kilograms of explosives were also recovered from the terrorists during that operation. In Khuzdar district, one terrorist was killed, the ISPR added.Balochistan, which borders Afghanistan, has seen a surge in abductions and attacks on civilians and security forces in recent years, prompting the government to step up its anti-militant operations.On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers near Mastung, on the Quetta-Karachi highway, and took them away. Their whereabouts remain unknown.On Sunday, at least 18 workers were abducted, and another was injured when unidentified armed men attacked a marble mining site in the province. The incident happened early in the morning in the remote Naal area of Khuzdar district, police said. The attackers arrived on motorcycles and other vehicles and stormed the site.According to PTI, no insurgent group or individual has claimed responsibility for the attack.The police and the provincial government have yet to confirm the incident officially, but two police officers, speaking on condition of anonymity, said 18 workers had been taken away by the attackers. PTI reported."They came on bikes and vehicles and opened fire and then rounded up the workers present at the site and abducted 18 of them before fleeing," a police officer said.Most of those abducted came from nearby villages and areas, he added, and another worker was injured in the attack.You use AI every day. articles.title: After deluge, Chennai likely to see lighter rain on Ayudha Puja
articles.summary: Chennai to get lighter rain for Ayudha Puja as cyclonic circulation weakens; yellow alert continues with heavy rain possible till Thursday after deluge.
articles.body: Chennai: Chennai residents can celebrate Ayudha Puja on Monday without worrying much about rain spoiling the festivities, as Regional Meteorological Centre has forecast reduced rainfall over the city and suburbs. The upper-air cyclonic circulation that triggered heavy rain on Saturday night is expected to move south and weaken, reducing the likelihood of heavy rainfall in Chennai until Tuesday.While RMC has forecast very heavy rainfall in the Western Ghats region on Wednesday, Chennai and surrounding districts will remain under yellow alert, with a warning for heavy rainfall until Thursday.RMC had earlier issued a red alert for Chennai district and an orange alert for Tiruvallur and Chengalpet on Sunday, anticipating extremely heavy rainfall exceeding 20cm as on Saturday. It later withdrew the alert in the evening and issued a fresh yellow alert. It was a bright sunny day in the city for the most part, with both Nungambakkam and Meenambakkam recording 32.2°C on Sunday.“The upper-air cyclonic circulation over north Tamil Nadu and adjoining south coastal Andhra Pradesh, which caused heavy rainfall in Chennai and suburbs on Saturday night, started weakening on Sunday afternoon. We anticipated the system to stay stable and issued the red alert for Sunday as per standard operating procedure due to flood risk, as the ground would have been saturated by absorbing the previous day’s rain,” said V R Durai, head of the regional weather forecasting center.Weather blogger Pradeep John said Chennai had not witnessed back-to-back 20cm rainfall from an upper air circulation (uac) without a break in the past. It may be noted that the Tamil Nadu state disaster management authority issued a personal warning to residents of Chennai to stay indoors following India Meteorological Department’s red alert.However, both the weather experts and IMD failed to forecast the magnitude of Saturday’s precipitation as north Chennai recorded more than 30cm of rainfall. Parry’s Corner recorded the highest rainfall at 36.3cm, followed by Kathivakkam with 34.4cm.
